strengths: The proposed GPG method is extremely simple and practical: it strips GRPO down to a plain policy gradient with group-normalized advantages, removing the critic, reference model, clipping, and KL penalty, which meaningfully reduces memory and implementation complexity.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering both unimodal mathematical reasoning (five benchmarks, multiple model scales: 1.5B, 7B) and multimodal tasks (visual reasoning, geometry, classification, grounding) across multiple established codebases (Open-r1, Open-rs, R1-V, Visual-RFT, VisualThinker-R1-Zero), which strengthens the external validity of the comparison against GRPO.

Useful ablations are provided: group size sensitivity, reward normalization scope (group vs. batch), and adding back a KL constraint (shown to hurt), plus training curves comparing loss, reward, and completion length.
The paper is clearly written and easy to follow; Table 1 and Table 11 give a clean component-wise comparison against PPO, GRPO, Dr. GRPO, and DAPO; code is open-sourced.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: GPG is essentially vanilla REINFORCE with a group-relative baseline. The 'contribution' of removing the clip term and KL penalty from GRPO is already well-trodden; RLOO, REINFORCE++, and Dr. GRPO move in the same direction, and the framing that GPG 'directly optimizes the original RL objective' while prior work only optimizes surrogates is a mischaracterization — Eq. 5 is still a Monte Carlo policy-gradient estimator, not the original objective, and the resulting gradient is the standard PG estimator.

Missing key baselines: the paper compares against GRPO and Dr. GRPO but omits RLOO and REINFORCE++, which are the closest prior methods; without these, it is hard to attribute the gains to the proposed design rather than to hyperparameter or implementation effects.

Evaluation rigor concerns: no multiple seeds, error bars, or variance estimates are reported, despite small evaluation sets (e.g., AIME24 with 30 problems, AMC23 with 40) where differences of a few points are well within noise; some results are mixed (GPG underperforms GRPO on Minerva in Table 2, and underperforms Dr. GRPO on AIME24 and MATH-500 in Table 3), which is glossed over in favor of aggregate claims of 'superior performance with clear margins.'

The central claim — that surrogate losses and trust-region constraints are unnecessary and even harmful — lacks any theoretical or analytical support. There is no investigation of when unconstrained updates fail (e.g., larger models, longer horizons, off-policy reuse), and the evaluation is limited to relatively small models and short training runs, weakening the scalability narrative.

Gains over GRPO are modest in the unimodal setting (1.6–2.6% average) relative to the strong claims in the abstract and introduction; the large multimodal improvements (e.g., +9.6 on CV-Bench, +14 mIoU on LISA) are surprising and would benefit from deeper analysis of the mechanism rather than a single qualitative case study.

Writing and presentation issues: several inconsistencies and typos ('evluate', 'achieves superior performance than', 'PGP' in the appendix), unequal compute/allocation details for baselines are under-specified, and the claimed computational-cost savings are asserted but never quantified with wall-clock or GPU-hour comparisons.

strengths: The paper is well motivated by the practical goal of reducing the computational footprint of RL fine-tuning for LLM/MLLM reasoning, and the proposed method (GPG) is simple to describe and easy to implement (Algorithm 1 is essentially a few lines).

The evaluation covers a relatively broad range of settings: two unimodal math setups (1.5B and 7B models) and several multimodal tasks (visual reasoning, geometry, classification, grounding), using established codebases (Open-r1, Open-rs, R1-V, Visual-RFT, VisualThinker-R1-Zero) for comparability.

Some useful ablations are provided, including group size sensitivity, group vs. batch reward normalization, and the effect of re-adding a KL constraint, plus qualitative training curves and a case study.
The authors state that code and implementation details are open-sourced, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: GPG is essentially vanilla REINFORCE with GRPO's group-normalized advantage. Removing the clip term and KL penalty to obtain a plain log-probability PG objective is a well-known, trivial configuration, and closely related simplifications (REINFORCE++ [19], ReMax [27], Dr. GRPO [30], DAPO's removal of the KL term) are not adequately compared experimentally. The framing that GPG 'directly optimizes the original RL objective' while prior methods only optimize 'surrogate losses' is misleading: the log-probability objective with a normalized-advantage baseline is exactly a policy-gradient estimator of the same objective and enjoys no special theoretical status.

The central claim of 'superior performance without relying on auxiliary techniques' rests on single-run results without variance estimates, seeds, or statistical significance. Several reported margins are small (e.g., +1.6% on Qwen2.5-Math-7B) and within plausible run-to-run noise, while other entries are internally inconsistent with the text (e.g., in Table 3 GPG trails GRPO on AMC23 by 2.5 points, yet the text claims superiority 'across four datasets' and elsewhere reuses AMC23 +10% as evidence).

Suspiciously large and unexplained multimodal gains undermine credibility: +9.6 points over GRPO on CV-Bench and >10-point improvements on LISA grounding with only 239 training images are extraordinary relative to the unimodal gains, and the paper offers no analysis of why removing stabilization mechanisms helps so much more in the multimodal setting. The single cherry-picked case study (Fig. 2) is not adequate support.
Missing key baseline: no comparison against REINFORCE++ or plain REINFORCE with the same group baseline, which is the closest method and essential to isolate what, if anything, is novel in GPG.

The claim of 'significantly reducing computational costs' is never substantiated with concrete measurements (wall-clock time, GPU memory, tokens processed); removing the reference model saves memory, but GPG also appears to need more groups for stability (group-size ablation shows best results at 16), which could offset the savings.

Stability concerns are dismissed rather than analyzed. It is well documented that unconstrained PG on LLMs can collapse or drift; the paper acknowledges 'it's a bit strange without imposing any distribution constraints' but provides only one KL ablation and no evidence of robustness across longer training runs, larger models, or noisier rewards.

Fairness of comparison is questionable: hyperparameters are inherited from GRPO, and the authors simultaneously assert (i) they are 'suboptimal for our approach' and (ii) the comparison is 'meticulously controlled'. GPG should be run with its own tuned hyperparameters and GRPO with tuned hyperparameters for a convincing comparison.

Writing quality is below the bar for a top venue: typos ('evluate', 'alogrithm', 'PGPresults'), grammatical errors ('GPG directly optimize'), vague or rhetorical passages ('it's a bit strange without imposing any distribution constraints'), and an incomplete abstract/code link. Table 4 baselines include misreported or garbled figures (e.g., rStar-Math 78.4 on AIME24 but 26.7 average), which suggests insufficient care.

The 'directly optimizing the original problem vs. surrogate' dichotomy that motivates the paper is presented without formal analysis; no theoretical or empirical study explains why surrogate losses would be harmful, which weakens the paper's core narrative.
Scope is narrow: only small models (1.5B-7B), short training runs (50-100 global steps), and the authors themselves admit no evaluation at scale, limiting the significance of the scalability claims.

strengths: The proposed GPG method is extremely simple and easy to implement, removing the critic model, reference model, clipping term, and KL penalty from GRPO, which is appealing from a practical and scalability standpoint.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering both unimodal mathematical reasoning (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B, Qwen2.5-Math-7B) and a range of multimodal tasks (visual reasoning, geometry, classification, grounding), with comparisons to GRPO, SFT, Dr. GRPO, and other baselines.
Useful ablation studies are provided on group size, reward normalization strategy (group vs. batch), and adding a KL constraint, and the paper is open-sourced, supporting reproducibility.
Training-time analysis (loss, reward, completion length curves) and qualitative case studies help illustrate the method's behavior.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: GPG is essentially GRPO with the importance-sampling ratio, clipping, and KL term removed, i.e., plain REINFORCE with group-normalized advantages. This is a very incremental simplification and closely overlaps with existing work (REINFORCE++, ReMax, RLOO-style group baselines, Dr. GRPO), which the paper does not adequately differentiate or empirically compare against.

The central claim of 'directly optimizing the original RL objective' rather than a surrogate is overclaimed and under-justified. Dropping the probability ratio is only valid for a strictly on-policy single-update setting; the paper provides no theoretical analysis of bias introduced when multiple epochs/updates per batch are used, and no stability or convergence analysis to justify removing all policy constraints.

The claim that GPG 'consistently outperforms GRPO' is not supported by the evidence: results are mixed (e.g., Table 2: GPG is worse than GRPO on Minerva and ties on AIME24; Table 3: GPG is worse on MATH-500 and AMC23), and gains are often small (1.6-2.6% average) with no variance estimates, multiple seeds, or statistical significance tests.

Some reported improvements are surprisingly large for such a marginal algorithmic change (e.g., +9.6 points on CV-Bench, +14 points on LISA grounding), which raises concerns about experimental variance or hyperparameter confounds; the paper acknowledges using GRPO's 'suboptimal' hyperparameters, but this weakens the fairness of the comparison.
Missing comparison to the most directly relevant baseline, REINFORCE++ [19], and to RLOO, given that GPG is essentially a REINFORCE variant; the comparison against Dr. GRPO is also limited.

Ablations are incomplete: the group-size study suggests performance still improves at group size 16, undercutting the chosen setting of 8; the KL ablation and reward-normalization ablation are only run on one model/dataset.

Presentation issues: several typos and inconsistencies ('evluate', 'PGP' vs. 'GPG', 'GPGresults'), Figure 1 does not report all benchmark numbers, and the writing contains unsupported strong claims (e.g., 'breakthrough').

strengths: The proposed method is extremely simple and well-motivated: removing the surrogate/clipping term, KL constraint, critic, and reference model yields a minimal policy-gradient baseline for LLM reasoning, and the paper convincingly demonstrates that such simplicity is sufficient to match or beat GRPO/DAPO.

Broad and fairly thorough empirical evaluation: multiple model scales (1.5B, 7B), base vs. distilled models, five math benchmarks, four multimodal tasks (geometry, classification, visual reasoning, grounding), comparisons against recent baselines (Dr. GRPO, Oat-Zero, SimpleRL-Zero, DAPO, Open-RS), and efficiency/cost reporting.

The analysis of the gradient-scale bias when many samples in a batch produce zero advantage is a useful practical observation, and the proposed alpha-correction plus valid-sample thresholding/resampling is a reasonable, cheap mitigation. The component-wise ablation (Table 15) cleanly attributes gains to each piece.

Robustness checks strengthen the empirical claims: pass@1/3/5 with mean and standard deviation over four random seeds, group-size sensitivity, reward-normalization ablation, KL-constraint ablation, and general-capability checks (MMLU, C-Eval, MBPP, HellaSwag) showing no degradation.
Good reproducibility posture: builds on public frameworks (VERL, open-r1, R1-V, Visual-RFT), documents hyperparameters, and commits to releasing code.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The core method is essentially REINFORCE with group-mean-centered advantages (closely related to RLOO, REINFORCE++, ReMax, and Dr. GRPO's unnormalized variant). The paper's main deltas—the alpha rescaling and thresholding—are small engineering refinements rather than a fundamentally new algorithm; positioning relative to RLOO/REINFORCE++ in experiments is missing.

The 'accurate gradient estimation' claim is mathematically fuzzy. Scaling the loss by alpha = B/(B-M) is equivalent to an adaptive per-batch learning-rate rescale; whether this yields an 'unbiased' gradient in any meaningful sense (given the objective itself is being rescaled) is not rigorously justified, and the argument that std-normalization 'introduces reward bias' conflates adaptive step-size normalization with statistical bias of the estimator.

Several headline claims rest on small-sample benchmarks with large variance: AMC23 has only 40 items, so the reported 22.3-point margin over SimpleRL-Zero corresponds to a handful of problems; the multimodal gains (e.g., +16.68 on CV-Bench, +14 on grounding) are surprisingly large and reported from single runs without confidence intervals.

The thresholding/resampling mechanism introduces a new hyperparameter (beta_th) with only two values ablated (0.6, 0.8) and near-identical results, leaving its sensitivity and interaction with alpha underexplored; the variance-unbiasing trade-off is not analyzed.

Hyperparameters are inherited from GRPO ('despite their suboptimality for our approach'); a proper tuning study for GPG, or symmetric tuning effort for baselines, is not reported, which slightly weakens fairness of comparisons.

Presentation issues: notation/typo inconsistencies (e.g., 'GPRO' for GRPO in tables), an objective in Eq. 5 whose normalization details are hard to reconcile with Algorithm 1, and several references with implausible dates/venues (e.g., ICLR 2026, arXiv IDs 2601.xxxxx) that raise citation-hygiene concerns.
Scaling claims (removing critic/reference for 'scalability') are not tested beyond 7B; the paper acknowledges this limitation, but the central efficiency/scalability argument remains extrapolative.

strengths: The proposed method is extremely simple (essentially vanilla policy gradient with group-mean baseline), and the paper is transparent about its components, with a clean component-by-component evolution table (Table 15) tracing GRPO to GPG.

The paper covers a broad empirical surface: unimodal math reasoning on 1.5B and 7B models, multimodal reasoning/classification/grounding tasks, ablations on group size, reward normalization, threshold beta_th, KL constraint, and efficiency comparisons with DAPO.

Appendix includes pass@3/pass@5 results with mean and standard deviation over four seeds, and a check of general capabilities (MMLU, C-Eval) to show reasoning gains do not degrade general performance.
The observation about all-right/all-wrong groups contributing zero gradient, and the resulting effective-batch rescaling, is a correct and practical implementation-level insight.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. GPG is essentially REINFORCE with a group-mean baseline, closely related to existing methods such as RLOO, ReMax, and GRPO-without-std (already explored in Dr. GRPO). The core 'contribution' is removing the std normalization, the ratio, and the KL term; these removals have been studied or implied in prior work (RLOO, Dr. GRPO, DAPO's dynamic sampling), and the paper does not adequately differentiate against RLOO/REINFORCE++, which are the natural and missing baselines.

The central empirical claim is weak on the authors' own evidence. In Table 1, GPG with Fnorm=1 and no AGE achieves 43.9% vs GRPO's 43.7% — within noise. The final gain comes from the alpha=B/(B-M) rescaling and the beta_th thresholding, which are essentially variance-reduction/batch-scaling tricks, not a fundamentally better algorithm. The paper even acknowledges this contradiction with its own 'no reward bias' argument, since Fnorm=std (i.e., GRPO-style normalization) outperforms Fnorm=1 in their ablations.

The 'unbiased gradient' framing is misleading. Dropping the importance-sampling ratio while taking multiple gradient steps per batch (standard in GRPO-style training) introduces off-policy bias that PPO's ratio/clipping was designed to control; the paper claims to optimize the 'original RL objective' but never analyzes multi-epoch behavior or policy-ratio drift.

Evaluation relies heavily on tiny benchmarks where single-problem differences are large: AIME24 (30 problems, so ~3.3% per problem), AMC23 (40 problems, ~2.5%). Headline claims like 'exceeding SimpleRL-Zero by 22.3% on AMC23' correspond to a handful of problems. Main-table pass@1 results lack seed variance; the multi-seed statistics only appear in the appendix for a subset of metrics, and pass@1 std is absent where the headline claims are made.

Multimodal results are suspiciously large and under-explained: +16.7 points on CV-Bench and +14 mIoU on LISA over GRPO with the same hyperparameters would be a remarkable finding for what is a small loss modification; no analysis, training curves for these tasks, or investigation of failure/instability modes is provided, which raises concerns about tuning asymmetry or evaluation artifacts.

Missing important baselines and hyperparameter fairness caveats: no RLOO, ReMax, REINFORCE++, or PPO comparisons; the claim of '0.45x training cost' vs DAPO is not backed by a rigorous accounting of identical hardware/steps/data, and 'NPUs from China' vs H20 GPUs makes cost comparisons across setups murky.

Clarity and polish issues: the abstract/intro oversell ('directly optimizes the original RL objective', 'SOTA results') relative to what is a delta on GRPO; the Project Page link is empty; typos ('EVALUTAION', 'GPRO' vs GRPO inconsistency in tables); the case study (Figure 4) is a single cherry-picked example in which the GPG answer (480) happens to match ground truth but the reasoning shown is largely hand-wavy.

The thresholding/resampling mechanism introduces a new hyperparameter (beta_th) whose sensitivity is studied only at two values (0.6, 0.8), and its interaction with alpha is not analyzed; combined with group-size sensitivity, the method is less 'hyperparameter-free' than the framing suggests.

strengths: The paper presents a genuinely minimalist RL recipe for LLM reasoning (no critic, no reference model, no KL, no clipped surrogate), and this simplicity makes the method easy to implement and cheap to train.

The experimental coverage is broad and mostly well executed: math benchmarks at 1.5B and 7B scale, five multimodal tasks (geometry, classification, CV-Bench, grounding), ablations over group size, normalization, threshold, an efficiency comparison against DAPO, general-capability checks on MMLU/C-Eval/code/QA, and pass@1/3/5 over four seeds with mean and standard deviation (Table 16).
The multi-seed results (Table 16) show consistent trends across pass@1/3/5, which partially mitigates concerns about high-variance benchmarks like AIME24.

The observation that GRPO's std normalization implicitly acts as a form of gradient correction, and the analysis of zero-gradient groups in distributed training (Appendix A), is a useful practical insight for practitioners.
A reproducibility statement, detailed hyperparameters, and an anonymous code release are provided.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The method is essentially REINFORCE with a group-mean baseline plus a batch-level rescaling by the fraction of valid (non-zero-gradient) samples. Both ingredients are close to known ideas (REINFORCE/RLOO family; valid-batch corrections and dynamic resampling as in DAPO), and the alpha = B/(B-M) correction is a fairly trivial fix once the zero-gradient issue is identified.

The central 'reward bias' narrative is not supported by the paper's own evidence. Removing the std normalization (Fnorm=1) yields 43.9 vs GRPO's 43.7 — essentially no gain — while the Fnorm=std variant (45.3) is the best configuration before AGE. This contradicts the claim that the std term should be removed as 'biased' and weakens the theoretical motivation; the actual gains come from alpha-scaling and thresholding, not from 'optimizing the original RL objective'.

Scale and strength of baselines are limited. All experiments are at 1.5B–7B; no larger models are tested (acknowledged in limitations). Some reproduced baselines are notably lower than their published numbers (e.g., Oat-Zero reproduced at 47.8 vs 51.4 reported), and the reported 6.3-point gap over Oat-Zero-7B rests partly on comparisons against reproduced rather than reported results.

The magnitude of the headline 7B result (57.7 average, 82.5 on AMC23, a >22-point jump over SimpleRL-Zero) is surprisingly large relative to the small methodological delta, and no pass@1 statistics with error bars are reported in Table 4; similarly, multimodal jumps (e.g., +16.7 on CV-Bench, +14 on grounding over GRPO) are much larger than the mathematical-reasoning deltas, raising questions about hidden hyperparameter or configuration differences.

The thresholding/resampling mechanism introduces a new hyperparameter (beta_th) whose ablation (0.6 vs 0.8) shows small, non-monotonic differences, so its necessity and robustness are not clearly established.

Writing and presentation issues: repeated typos (e.g., 'GPRO' in Tables 1 and 15, 'Evalutaion' in Section 3.3), low-resolution figures, and several references with implausible or future-dated identifiers (e.g., arXiv:2601.xxxxx, ICLR/AAAI 2026 entries) that should be carefully verified.

There is no theoretical or empirical analysis of failure modes of dropping all policy constraints (e.g., training instability over longer horizons, off-policy drift when multiple minibatch epochs are used), which is the main risk of a 'no-surrogate, no-KL' method.
